clue.text: People are not inclined to believe in this attitude

definitions.text: People are not inclined to believe in this attitude

blocks.clueFragment: People are not inclined to believe in
blocks.note: surface reading: a description of a creed or cause that fails to win followers
setter's reading: the attitude itself is the refusal to believe, a doubting frame of mind

explanation.surface: A commentator laments a stance that nobody takes seriously.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as if people reject some attitude, but the attitude is the not-believing itself: SCEPTICISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Scepticism is a habitual doubt, an unwillingness to accept claims without proof.

indicators.note: letters put to trouble are thrown into disorder and must be sorted out again

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman who was once in a scrape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is fodder alongside 'once' and only 'trouble' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Connie is a female first name, short for Constance, so it serves as an example of a girl.

blocks.note: the prefix meaning before
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A churchgoer shows off by arriving before ten o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretence can mean a showy display or affectation, which is what ostentation is.

blocks.note: surface reading: a dossier or archive kept in the Indian capital
setter's reading: advancing one at a time, people walking in a single line

explanation.surface: An official document from Delhi charting some unusual advance.
explanation.walkthrough: A file kept in India would be an Indian file; INDIAN FILE also means a line of people moving one behind another.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian file is an old phrase for single file, a column walking one person behind another.

clue.text: On whom (or where) coals of fire may be heaped?

definitions.text: On whom (or where) coals of fire may be heaped?

blocks.note: setter's reading: the biblical heaping of coals of fire on someone, repaying unkindness with kindness to shame them

blocks.clueFragment: (or where) coals of fire may be heaped
blocks.note: second reading: the place in a fireplace where burning coals are piled

explanation.surface: A question about the proper target of a biblical rebuke.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN GRATE, the answer is where coals sit in a hearth; whole, it is the ungrateful person shamed by kindness (Romans 12:20).
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, the classic recipient of good returned for evil.

blocks.note: surface reading: an athlete competing in a qualifying race
setter's reading: to run as wax or butter does when warmed and turns liquid

explanation.surface: A sprinter lines up in the early rounds of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heat' wants to be a race; it is warmth, and running is what softened solids do.
explanation.definitionFit: To melt is to turn liquid under warmth, so that the substance runs.

clue.text: Cut-out action when noise - rises around 91

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the word comes backwards
around means wrapping one piece about another, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
91 in Roman numerals: XC (90) plus I (1)

explanation.surface: A cut-out is triggered when the noise level climbs past a threshold.
explanation.walkthrough: Numbers in old clues often stand for Roman numerals; the reversed word is split after its first letter to take them in.
explanation.definitionFit: Excision is the act of cutting something out, as a surgeon removes tissue.

clue.text: 3 14's spirit to dance ? That's for suckers !

blocks.note: the spirit that begins the answer to 14 down
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A spirit leads to a dance, and only fools fall for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suckers' looks like dupes, but it means people who suck sweets; a brandy ball is a boiled sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy ball is a hard boiled sweet flavoured with brandy, made to be sucked slowly.

blocks.note: Methuselah is the Bible's oldest man, said to have lived 969 years
setter's reading: the drink that would explain such longevity, the fabled potion of life

explanation.surface: A joke question about what the long-lived patriarch liked to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Living that long suggests the elixir of life.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a magical potion, notably the legendary one granting endless life.

clue.text: A low  cur often has our sympathy

definitions.text: A low  cur often has our sympathy

blocks.note: surface reading: a base mongrel, a despicable hound
setter's reading: the competitor expected to lose, whom the crowd tends to support

explanation.surface: We feel sorry for a miserable stray dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Low gives UNDER and cur gives DOG; together they name the expected loser everyone roots for.
explanation.definitionFit: The underdog is the contestant thought least likely to win, who usually attracts popular support.

blocks.note: surface reading: a radical political rebel; setter's reading: to do with turning, like a wheel
a member of a club, here the service club whose emblem is a wheel

explanation.surface: A member of some insurgent society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a rebel; it means rotary, as in the Rotary Club, a worldwide service organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rotarian is a member of Rotary International, a businessmen's service club named for rotating meeting venues.

blocks.note: the four compass points, south, east, west and north

explanation.surface: A sailing boat zigzags every which way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tacked' suggests sailing, but it is loose stitching.
explanation.definitionFit: To tack is to stitch loosely with long temporary stitches, so tacked fabric has been stitched.

blocks.note: surface reading: the most tangible or real; setter's reading: solid
the virtue of standing together in unity

explanation.surface: A philosopher ranks the virtues by how tangible they are.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer begins SOLID, the most concrete-sounding of qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: Solidarity is unity and mutual support within a group, a commonly praised civic virtue.

clue.text: It isn't apparently, + makes a person distinguished

blocks.note: setter's reading: split up, the word seems to deny that someone has skill or talent
surface reading: the quality of being eminent or noteworthy

explanation.surface: Something that seems not to be what it is still brings a person honour.
explanation.walkthrough: NOTABILITY splits to NOT ABILITY, so it apparently isn't ability, yet it is distinction.
explanation.definitionFit: Notability is the state of being notable, prominent or eminent in public regard.

clue.text: Spirit photograph ? It takes the biscuit !

blocks.note: brandy is a distilled spirit
a snap is a casual photograph

explanation.surface: A picture of a ghost? That is the most outrageous thing yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is a British idiom for being the most outrageous; here it literally describes a biscuit. 'Spirit photograph' pretends to be a ghost picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a thin crisp rolled ginger biscuit, so it is literally a type of biscuit.

clue.text: A blooming underhand, attack by an essayist

definitions.note: a flowering plant, read as 'a bloomer'

blocks.note: a lob is an underarm throw or ball, a gentle lofted attack
Elia was the pen name of essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A blasted sneaky assault from a writer of essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like a mild British swear word; it means flowering. Elia is Charles Lamb's pen name, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobelia is a garden plant with small blue or purple flowers, a bedding favourite.

clue.text: The rotters are for the high jump

definitions.text: The rotters are for the high jump

blocks.clueFragment: The rotters are for the high jump
blocks.note: surface reading: the scoundrels are about to be punished, the British idiom 'for the high jump'
setter's reading: those who leap well, suited to the athletics event

explanation.surface: The cads are going to get what is coming to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the high jump' is a British idiom for being in serious trouble; the answer means both cads and good leapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounder is dated slang for a dishonourable man, a cad, and literally one who bounds or leaps.

clue.text: Get a man to change colour

indicators.note: changing the words means rearranging their letters into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Persuade a man to switch his colours, as a turncoat would.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red shade, named after a dye discovered around the battle of Magenta.

blocks.note: surface reading: teamed up, cooperated with someone
setter's reading: the armed services, which a recruit signs up for

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for collaborating is read literally as signing up to the army, navy or air force.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist is to sign up for military service, so an enlisted recruit has entered the services.

clue.text: Islander who could make it copyright

blocks.note: a native of a Mediterranean island republic
setter's reading: the letters of the answer rearrange to something that sounds like the legal term

explanation.surface: An island resident who might claim legal ownership of a work.
explanation.walkthrough: CYPRIOT rearranges to COPYRIT, which says the same as 'copyright'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cypriot is a native or inhabitant of Cyprus, an island in the eastern Mediterranean.

blocks.note: setter's reading: coloured twice over, first one shade and then another
surface reading: a scoundrel who has been beaten until bruised

explanation.surface: A rogue gets a thorough beating.
explanation.walkthrough: Black and blue are two dyes; the phrase for a utter rogue is DOUBLE-DYED.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-dyed means thoroughgoing or out-and-out, used of a confirmed villain.

indicators.note: in tells the solver the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone who stays loyal through every hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' looks like an anagram signal, but the answer is hidden across the two words. LEAL is Scots for loyal.
explanation.definitionFit: Leal is a Scottish and archaic word meaning loyal and true.

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who begins her morning; setter's reading: the dawn
a goddess, a divine being

explanation.surface: A woman who begins each morning beautifully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divinely' looks like praise, but it says she is a deity: the Roman goddess of the dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Aurora was the Roman goddess of dawn, and the word also means daybreak itself.

blocks.note: surface reading: a gift brought to a party celebrating a new home
setter's reading: a car component that also heats rooms

explanation.surface: A driver brings a present to a new-home party.
explanation.walkthrough: A car has one under the bonnet, and a house uses one to warm itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A radiator is both a car's engine-cooling unit and a domestic heater warming a room.

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thanks
the same word repeated

explanation.surface: Saying thanks once more on parting.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is British slang for thank you; ta-ta is a casual farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is an informal British farewell, equivalent to bye-bye or cheerio.

blocks.note: surface reading: the secret to freedom of travel
setter's reading: the key a driver turns to start the engine

explanation.surface: The secret to freedom on the highway.
explanation.walkthrough: The key that starts a car is the ignition key.
explanation.definitionFit: The ignition is the system that fires a car engine, switched on by its key.

clue.text: The rat can be a real menace

indicators.note: can be suggests the words may become something else once their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rats are a genuine danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat is something likely to cause harm or danger, exactly what a menace is.

blocks.note: surface reading: holding totally contrary opinions
setter's reading: someone living on the exact opposite side of the globe

explanation.surface: Someone who disagrees with everything we stand for.
explanation.walkthrough: From Britain, the far side of the earth is Australia and New Zealand, whose people are called this.
explanation.definitionFit: An antipodean lives at the antipodes, the point on Earth directly opposite, typically Australia.
